title: Beating Jet Lag: What Actually Works, According to the Evidence
metaDescription: A science-based jet lag protocol — light timing, melatonin, meal timing and sleep strategy — plus the popular remedies that do not work.
excerpt: Jet lag is a circadian problem, not a tiredness problem. Which means the fix is light and timing, not sleep and coffee.
author: Travel Editors
content:
Jet lag is not exhaustion. You can be perfectly rested and still have it, because the problem is not how much you slept — it is that your internal clock is telling your body it is 4am while the sun outside insists it is lunchtime.

That distinction matters, because it points at the fix. Sleeping more does not resynchronise a circadian rhythm. **Light does.** Everything else is a supporting act.

## Why Direction Matters More Than Distance

Your body clock runs slightly longer than 24 hours naturally, which means it finds **lengthening** a day easier than shortening one.

- **Travelling west** — you are staying up later. Generally easier. Expect roughly one day of adjustment per time zone, often faster.
- **Travelling east** — you are going to bed earlier, which your body resists. Generally harder. Expect around a day and a half per time zone.

A six-hour eastward flight — Europe to India, the US to Europe — is meaningfully harder than the same journey in reverse. Plan more recovery time on eastward trips and schedule anything important later in the visit.

Crossing fewer than three time zones rarely produces significant jet lag. Beyond about eight, you are likely to feel it regardless of what you do, though the protocol below shortens it substantially.

## The Thing That Actually Works: Light Timing

Light is the dominant signal your circadian system uses, and **when** you get it determines which way your clock moves.

The principle:

- **Light in the morning** at your destination **advances** your clock — it shifts you earlier. This is what you want when travelling **east**.
- **Light in the evening delays** your clock — shifts you later. This is what you want when travelling **west**.
- **Light at the wrong time actively pushes you the wrong way.** This is why some people feel worse after a day outdoors.

**Travelling east:** seek bright light in the morning at your destination, and avoid it in the late evening. Get outside early, even if it is the last thing you feel like.

**Travelling west:** seek light in the late afternoon and evening, and avoid bright morning light for the first day or two. Sunglasses in the morning genuinely help here.

Outdoor daylight is many times brighter than indoor lighting, even on an overcast day. A walk outside is far more effective than sitting by a window.

## Melatonin: Useful, and Usually Taken Wrong

Melatonin has reasonable evidence for jet lag, particularly eastward travel. Two things are commonly misunderstood.

**It is a timing signal, not a sleeping pill.** Melatonin tells your body it is night. It does not sedate you meaningfully. People take a large dose expecting to be knocked out, feel nothing, and conclude it does not work.

**Dose low, and time it correctly.** The evidence suggests **0.5mg to 3mg** taken shortly before your target bedtime at the destination. Larger doses are commonly sold and are not more effective — they are more likely to cause grogginess.

Timing: for eastward travel, take it in the early evening at destination time, starting on arrival or a day or two before departure. For westward travel, melatonin is less useful; light timing does more.

Melatonin is regulated differently across countries — prescription-only in some, freely available in others. Check before travelling with it, and speak to a doctor if you are pregnant, on other medication, or have a medical condition.

## What to Do on the Flight

**Set your watch to destination time when you board.** Then behave according to that time, not the time you left. This single mental shift drives every other decision.

**Sleep if it is night at your destination. Stay awake if it is day.** Even if that means staying awake on a night flight, or trying to sleep at what feels like mid-afternoon.

**Skip the alcohol.** It is sedating but it fragments sleep badly and dehydrates. A glass of wine on a long-haul flight costs more sleep quality than it buys.

**Be strategic with caffeine.** Useful to stay awake when you need to be awake at destination time. Actively harmful in the eight hours before your target sleep window — caffeine's half-life means an afternoon coffee is still in your system at midnight.

**Drink water consistently.** Cabin humidity is very low. Dehydration will not cause jet lag but it makes every symptom worse.

**Move.** Walk the cabin every couple of hours, stretch, and do ankle circles in your seat. This is about circulation and comfort rather than circadian rhythm, but it materially affects how you feel on landing.

**Use the tools.** Eye mask, earplugs or noise-cancelling headphones, and a neck pillow that actually supports your head. The difference between three hours of broken sleep and five hours of decent sleep on a long-haul flight is mostly equipment.

![Travel Tips travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1776624347201-73c277dc2bc2?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## The First Day at Your Destination

This is the day that determines the rest of the trip.

- **Do not nap for more than 20 minutes**, and not after mid-afternoon. A long afternoon nap on day one is the single most common cause of a week of disrupted nights.
- **If you must nap, set an alarm.** Twenty minutes restores alertness without entering deep sleep.
- **Get outside**, at the right time for your direction of travel.
- **Eat meals at local times**, even if you are not hungry. Meal timing is a secondary circadian signal and it helps.
- **Exercise moderately** — a walk, a swim. Not a hard session, which will make the fatigue worse.
- **Stay up until a reasonable local bedtime**, ideally 9 or 10pm. Going to bed at 6pm guarantees a 2am wake-up.
- **Expect to wake in the night.** It is normal for the first few nights. Do not panic, do not check the time repeatedly, and do not reach for your phone — screen light at 3am actively works against you.

## Pre-Adjusting Before You Fly

For important trips — a wedding, a conference, anything where you need to function on day one — shifting your schedule before departure helps significantly.

Three or four days out, move your sleep and wake times by an hour a day toward destination time. Eastward: go to bed and wake earlier. Westward: later. Combine with light exposure at the corresponding times.

It is a nuisance and it genuinely works. Even a partial shift of two hours removes two days of adjustment.

## What Does Not Work

- **"Sleeping it off."** Extra sleep does not resynchronise a clock. You can sleep twelve hours and still feel wrong at the wrong times.
- **Most jet lag supplements and homeopathic remedies.** No credible evidence.
- **Grounding, special diets and elaborate fasting protocols.** The fasting research is interesting and preliminary; the commercial protocols built on it overstate it considerably.
- **Sleeping pills as a strategy.** They produce sleep without shifting the clock, and the grogginess often outlasts the benefit. Occasionally useful on a specific flight; not a solution.
- **Powering through with caffeine.** It masks the symptom and delays the adjustment.

## A Realistic Expectation

Even done perfectly, crossing eight or more time zones takes several days to fully resolve. The protocol above typically halves it, which on a one-week trip is the difference between three good days and six.

For short trips of two or three days across many time zones, the pragmatic alternative is **not to adjust at all** — stay on home time as far as your schedule allows, and accept being nocturnal. Adjusting and then immediately un-adjusting is worse than never adjusting.

If you are travelling as a group, one more thing worth agreeing in advance: **day one should be empty.** The temptation to schedule something on arrival day is strong and it is almost always a mistake. Building a deliberately blank first day into the shared plan — easy to do in **Trypinn**, and easy to skip if you do not write it down — protects the rest of the trip from the consequences.
